fichas.title: Functional Scheme of an Airport Terminal
fichas.summary: The theoretical terminal scheme separates landside and airside functions and coordinates passenger, baggage, and transit flows. It shows departure and arrival routes, including check-in, safety and passport controls, customs, luggage pick-up, waiting areas, commercial areas, and transport or boarding-bridge connections. Non-Schengen passengers and transit luggage are also represented.

fichas.title: Terminal and Ground-Access Configurations
fichas.summary: Sectional diagrams compare terminal arrangements and their relationship to roads, aircraft, boarding bridges, and, in one example, an urban rail link. The illustrated configurations include a ground-level road with a single-floor terminal on the same level; ground-level roads with two-storey terminals; a road on two levels with a two-storey terminal; and a road on two levels with an urban rail link and a three-storey terminal with a service floor. The diagrams distinguish arriving passengers, departing passengers, and luggage.

fichas.title: Terminal Handling, Security, and Non-Aviation Functions
fichas.summary: Terminal design balances complex technical and functional requirements, including separation of public and secure areas, handling-area organization, movement and waiting zones, and multi-storey conveyor routes. Passenger handling extends from check-in through security controls to boarding and may be carried out by an airline or a handling agent. Security requires that unchecked passengers and baggage cannot access an aircraft and that checked and unchecked passengers do not come into contact. National and international, including Schengen and non-Schengen, passenger flows require separation and multiple routes and controls; routes should be quick and short. Non-aviation activities such as hotels, congress centres, shopping, and restaurants must be balanced with efficient passenger procedures and strategically positioned commercial areas.
